implementation_notes: The @dataclass decorator replaces the handwritten value class: field annotations plus generated __init__/__eq__/__repr__, with frozen=True giving immutability at the language level, and dataclasses.asdict() recursively converts the instance (including nested dataclasses) into the dict that json.dumps serialises. On the return path the payload must be validated explicitly, because dataclasses do no type checking. Keep this stdlib-only form as the default: it is explicit about the wire shape, cheap to construct and adds no dependency.
code_sketch:
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class OrderDTO:
    id: int
    customer: str
    lines: list[LineDTO]

wire = json.dumps(asdict(dto))          # -> JSON text
dto = OrderDTO(**json.loads(wire))      # no runtime type checking
pitfalls: No validation and no coercion: JSON supplies int/str/list and the dataclass accepts whatever is passed (OrderDTO(id="1") is legal), so untrusted payloads need a validating layer.
asdict() deep-copies recursively and calls copy.deepcopy on unknown members, which fails on non-dataclass or non-copyable values (datetime, Decimal, numpy arrays) - provide a custom default handler.
Mutable defaults require field(default_factory=...) and equality is class-sensitive: a dict with identical data is never equal to the dataclass instance.

variants.name: TypedDict payload over a plain dict
variants.implementation_notes: When the payload should stay a plain dict, for maximum interop with json, existing code and third-party APIs, TypedDict declares its shape for the type checker at zero runtime cost: the DTO is the dict itself and mypy/pyright catch key typos and type drift. Nothing is validated or converted at runtime, so this is the realization for trusted, fully typed producers and consumers; add a validator when the boundary is not trusted.
variants.code_sketch:
from typing import TypedDict

class OrderDTO(TypedDict):
    id: int
    customer: str
    lines: list[LineDTO]

payload: OrderDTO = json.loads(wire)   # static typing only, no runtime check
pitfalls: TypedDict instances are ordinary dicts at runtime: nothing prevents missing or extra keys, and json.loads returns dict[str, Any] that only the type checker treats as the DTO.
total=False and Required/NotRequired are easy to get wrong, and a typo in a string key is invisible unless the code is type-checked in CI.

variants.name: Validating model (Pydantic v2)
variants.implementation_notes: The validation-first realization used by most modern Python HTTP services: the DTO is a BaseModel whose annotations are enforced and coerced at runtime, model_validate_json parses and validates in one step (raising ValidationError with precise field locations), model_dump_json produces the wire form and model_json_schema exports the contract. It replaces the dataclass when untrusted input must be rejected rather than silently accepted, and pydantic-core makes it fast enough for request-sized payloads.
variants.code_sketch:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class OrderDTO(BaseModel):
    id: int
    customer: str
    lines: list[LineDTO] = []

dto = OrderDTO.model_validate_json(wire)   # parse + validate
wire_back = dto.model_dump_json()
pitfalls: Coercion means an invalid payload may be silently repaired (extra keys dropped, defaults filled, "1" turned into 1) - pin the model config and test the rejection paths.
The v2 API differs from v1 (model_validate/model_dump instead of parse_obj/dict) and the model is tied to the library's validation semantics, so upgrading is a real migration.
